does: Cooks a pale roux, whisks warm milk into it a little at a time and simmers it to a smooth white sauce seasoned with nutmeg. Thin, it coats food. Thick, it holds a baked dish together.

intro.what: Béchamel joins milk to a pale roux and simmers it into a smooth white sauce.
intro.why: It teaches you to add liquid gradually and choose thickness for coating food or binding a baked dish.

how: Warm the milk in a second pan until it is hot but not boiling.
Melt the butter in a saucepan, stir in an equal weight of flour and cook it, stirring, only until it smells like biscuit and has taken no colour.
Take the pan off the heat and whisk in a ladle of milk until the paste is smooth. Add the rest a ladle at a time, whisking each one smooth.
Set the pan back on a low heat and simmer gently, stirring into the corners, until the raw taste of flour has gone and the sauce coats a spoon.
Season with salt and a grating of nutmeg. For a baked dish, cook it thicker. For coating, leave it looser.
If it must wait, press a piece of buttered paper onto its surface so that no skin forms.

cues.text: The sauce is smooth and ivory, and runs off the spoon in a slow, even ribbon.
The smell of raw flour has gone and a gentle smell of milk and nutmeg remains.

mistakes.mistake: Pouring in all the milk at once, which leaves lumps.
mistakes.fix: Add it a ladle at a time and whisk each one smooth. A lumpy sauce can be rescued through a sieve.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the sauce unstirred on the heat, so that it catches on the base of the pan.
mistakes.fix: Stir into the corners all the while and keep the heat low.

mistakes.mistake: Serving it before the flour is cooked out, so that it tastes pasty.
mistakes.fix: Simmer it gently until it tastes of milk and not of flour.

quiz.question: How does the desired use affect the sauce thickness?
choices: Looser for coating, thicker for holding a baked dish together.
Always equally thick regardless of use.
Thinner for binding a baked dish than for coating.
quiz.because: Thickness serves the job: a coating sauce can be looser than a sauce that binds a dish.

quiz.question: How do you add milk to the pale roux?
choices: All at once before beginning to whisk.
Only after browning the roux dark.
quiz.because: Gradual additions help the paste join the milk smoothly instead of forming lumps.

quiz.question: Which appearance matches a smooth béchamel?
choices: Brown sauce with floating flour lumps.
Thin milk separated from a grainy paste.
Ivory sauce flowing in a slow, even ribbon.
quiz.because: A smooth ivory ribbon shows the milk and pale roux have combined.

quiz.question: The sauce is starting to stick at the base. What would you change?
choices: Keep the heat low and stir into the corners.
Raise the heat and stir only the surface.
Leave it still until a skin forms.
quiz.because: Gentle heat and stirring across the base and corners reduce catching.

comes_after.why: A béchamel begins with a pale roux, so a cook has to be able to cook flour in fat without lumps or colour.
